newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: OECD SAYS SEES SLOVAKIA AS NEXT MEMBER.
newsitem.headline: OECD SAYS SEES SLOVAKIA AS NEXT MEMBER.

text.p: Slovakia should become the next member of the Organisation For Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), but needs to make further steps such as privatising its financial sector, officials said on Monday.
"Slovakia should be the next member of the OECD," OECD secretary general Donald Johnston told a news conference after meetings with representatives of Finnish industry in Helsinki.
"There are several applicants (but) there are no imminent members except for Slovakia," he said, adding the examination process for Slovak membership was "quite far advanced."

Earlier, OECD Legal Department head Christian Shricke told Reuters in a telephone interview from OECD headquarters in Paris that Slovakia had taken many steps toward membership, though some outstanding issues were still to be addressed.
"...in the trade area, while there still are some issues of concern, there does not seem to be any significant stumbling block," Shricke said.

But, he added, in areas such as the liberalisation of capital movements and international investment instruments, "there still remain a number of issues on which we have not seen positive action from the Slovak authorities".

"Improvement is necessary for transparency, consistency and predictability in the implementation of investment related laws, and in the process of privatisation, particularly in the financial sectors," Shricke said.
"We encouraged authorities to proceed expeditiously with the privatisation of remaining state-owned assets in particular in the financial sectors," he added.
Privatisation in Slovakia, which hopes to gain entrance to the club of the world's wealthiest nations by the end of 1997, has been the most hotly-debated topic in recent months.

Last month it nearly tore apart the governing coalition when the ultra-left coalition party ZRS crossed the floor in parliament to vote with the opposition to approve a measure halting any bank sell-off until the end of the year 2003.
President Michal Kovac, at the government's request, has since returned the law to parliament for re-assessment, though the opposition and ZRS have said they will again approve it.
The state holds major stakes in the country's four largest financial institutions -- savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna, commercial banks VUB and IRB , and insurer Slovenska Poistovna .

Shricke said that while no one issue determines whether a country is accepted in the OECD, Slovakia must show it is committed to free market principles, and the extent to which effective market access is possible for foreign direct investors -- including the privatisation of state-owned assets.

"It is important for an authentic market economy that the major part of (it) is in private hands. Therefore as part of Slovakia's commitments to the basic tenets of market economy the extent to which the private sector is controlling the essential share in the economy is very relevant," he said.
Shricke added that no OECD member is expected to have 100 percent of its companies in private hands, "but the so-called strategic enterprises should be reduced to a minimum".

Slovakia has posted some of the strongest economic results of the nations to emerge from communist East Europe with 1996 GDP growth expected to reach nearly seven percent, and year-on-year inflation at a region-wide low of 5.8 percent.
But the country's image has suffered from Western rebukes that it is lagging behind in democratic reforms.
Shricke said that in the end, the country's image is less a factor than its adherence to OECD norms.
"If the overall picture is one that members believe demonstrates Slovkaia's commitment to the basic principles of the OECD's instruments, they will say yes," he said.
"If they believe these commitments fall short of it, they will say you still need to improve the position in one or more respects," he added.
